opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot. The way I see it, software engineering isn't just one vertical among many for us. It's really the foundation. If you can build agents that are genuinely autonomous at coding, you've essentially built agents that can operate a computer, because so much of what happens on a computer is ultimately mediated through code. So our view is that going deep on coding first is actually the most direct path to general capability, not a detour from it.

That said, we're pretty deliberate about not expanding too early. One of the lessons I took from my time working on things like Gemini and earlier on RL research is that breadth without depth tends to give you demos rather than products. You get something that looks impressive across a lot of tasks but isn't reliable enough on any one of them for people to actually hand over real work. So the bar we set for ourselves is: are customers trusting the agent with tasks they'd otherwise give to a skilled engineer? Until we're clearly there, expanding sideways would be a distraction.

When we do expand, I think it'll happen fairly naturally along the lines of where code already touches other work. Think about data analysis, operations, internal tooling, a lot of the knowledge work inside an enterprise that's really just glue between systems. Those are areas where a strong coding agent already has most of the skills it needs. It's more about context, permissions, and understanding the organization's specific environment than about fundamentally new capabilities.

And the other piece is the learning loop. The thing that I think matters most long term is building systems that get better from real usage in real environments, with real feedback signals. Coding is a great place to develop that because you have relatively clean signals: tests pass or fail, code gets merged or doesn't. If we can really nail how to turn that kind of feedback into continuous improvement, the methodology transfers to other domains, even ones where the reward signal is messier. So in a sense, the expansion plan is less about picking the next vertical and more about building the recipe for autonomy in one domain so well that applying it elsewhere becomes the obvious next step.

r001.rationale: The response says deep coding work can build general capability and stresses reliability, but does not identify deeper comprehension of software engineering as the means of producing more reliable coding agents.

r002.rationale: It sets customer trust in the coding agent as a threshold before expanding, but does not propose using customer demand to guide which areas Reflection expands into.

r003.rationale: It warns that breadth without depth yields unreliable demos and says expanding sideways before customers trust the coding agent with skilled-engineer tasks would be a distraction.

r004.rationale: It says adjacent enterprise work draws on coding-agent skills and requires organization-specific context, but does not argue that an organizational context core built for engineering provides the foundation for expansion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we started with software engineering not because we think coding is the end goal, but because it's the best training ground we have right now. Code is this really special domain where the feedback loops are tight. You write something, you run it, it either works or it doesn't. You have tests, you have compilers, you have execution traces. That gives you a verifiable signal, and verifiable signals are what reinforcement learning actually feeds on.

So when I think about expanding beyond it, I don't think of it as "okay, now we go do legal, now we go do finance." I think of it as: which capabilities that we're building in code are actually general? And the answer is most of them. Long-horizon planning, decomposing an ambiguous goal into steps, using tools, recovering when something breaks, knowing when to ask for help versus push through. None of that is coding-specific. It just happens that code is where you can measure it cleanly.

The way I'd frame the strategy is in layers. The first layer is domains that are adjacent and still verifiable. Things like data science, DevOps, security, scientific computing. Those still have a lot of the properties of code, you can check the answer, but the task distribution is broader and messier. That's a natural next step and frankly a lot of it falls out of the same training recipe.

The second layer is where it gets interesting and harder, which is domains where the reward is less crisp. Research, analysis, operating inside an enterprise where "did this work" depends on a human judgment or an outcome you only see weeks later. There I think the key insight is you can't just port the coding agent over. You have to figure out what the equivalent of the "unit test" is in that domain. Sometimes it's a simulator. Sometimes it's a model-based verifier. Sometimes it's a human in the loop but structured so that the feedback is dense enough to learn from. The research question at Reflection is really how do you manufacture verifiable environments for things that don't come with them natively.

And then the third thing I'd say, and this is more of a discipline than a strategy, is don't expand faster than the system actually earns it. The temptation in this space is to announce that your agent does everything. But the whole premise of what we're doing is that reliability comes from the training loop, not from the demo. So you go into a new domain when you have a real environment for it, real evaluations, and a path to improvement that isn't just prompting harder. If you can't close the loop, you're not ready.

The one thing I'd push back on in the framing is the idea of "beyond" software engineering as if it's a departure. I think the better mental model is that software is becoming the interface to everything. More and more of knowledge work is going to route through agents that write and execute code to get things done, even when the user never sees a line of it. So in some sense expanding beyond software engineering just means teaching the agent what the code is for, rather than teaching it something unrelated to code.

r001.rationale: It calls code a useful training ground and says reliability comes from the training loop, but does not identify deeper comprehension of software engineering as the means to produce more reliable coding agents.

r002.rationale: It recommends expanding when the system has real environments and evaluations, but does not propose using customer demand to guide expansion.

r003.rationale: It cautions against expanding too quickly, but does not identify pursuing adjacent opportunities before establishing a core category as a risk of diluting startup focus.

r004.rationale: It says software can become an interface for knowledge work, but does not argue that an organizational context core built for engineering can ground expansion into adjacent enterprise work.

astra-6.text:
I think the way to think about it is: what capabilities do we build through software engineering that transfer to other kinds of work? Because coding requires a lot more than generating code. You have to understand a goal, explore an unfamiliar environment, make a plan, use tools, and figure out whether what you did actually worked.

Those are pretty general capabilities. But I wouldn’t assume that being good at coding automatically makes you good at every other task. The feedback is different. In software, you can often run a test and get a fairly clear signal. In other domains, figuring out whether you’ve succeeded can be much harder.

So I’d expand into areas where we can close that feedback loop—where the model can take an action, observe the result, and improve. The ambition is broader than software engineering, but the way to get there is to make these systems reliable on increasingly general tasks, rather than just declare that they’re general.

r001.rationale: The response describes capabilities involved in coding and says systems should become more reliable on general tasks, but it does not identify deeper software engineering comprehension as a way to make coding agents more reliable.

r002.rationale: It recommends expanding into areas with a clear feedback loop, but does not propose using customer demand to guide expansion.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss adjacent opportunities diluting a startup’s focus or the risk of pursuing them before establishing a core category.

r004.rationale: It does not identify an organizational context core built for engineering as a foundation for adjacent enterprise work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think software engineering is the right place to start because you have this really powerful feedback loop: the model can do something, run it, see what happened, and improve. The question for expanding beyond that is where we can create similarly good feedback loops.

I wouldn’t think about it as, “We’ve done coding, now let’s build a separate product for every other profession.” I’d think about what capabilities transfer. Can the system work toward a goal over a long period of time? Can it use tools, check its own work, and recover when something goes wrong? Those capabilities are useful far beyond software engineering.

But you still have to ground them in a specific task. So I’d expand into areas where we can measure whether the agent actually accomplished something, learn from failures, and earn trust incrementally. The ambition can be broad, while the next step stays very concrete.

r001.rationale: The response highlights software engineering’s feedback loop and transferable capabilities, but does not say that deeper comprehension of software engineering produces more reliable coding agents.

r002.rationale: It recommends choosing areas with measurable outcomes and concrete tasks, but does not propose using customer demand to guide expansion.

r003.rationale: It cautions against building a separate product for every profession, but does not identify pursuing adjacent opportunities before establishing a core category as a risk of diluting focus.

r004.rationale: It mentions capabilities that transfer beyond software engineering, but does not argue that an organizational context core built for engineering can underpin adjacent enterprise work.
